confidence_note: From reviews and summaries, not the book text. Old text's opening examples (fasting animals, cold mice) and slogans ('biology thrives on hardship') dropped; no source ties them to the book. Much of the supporting evidence is animal or early research, flagged in the story.
facts: The survival circuit is a set of longevity genes inherited from the earliest life forms: sirtuins, mTOR and AMPK.
It evolved to get organisms through famine and cold winters.
In comfortable modern life it sits mostly dormant, in Sinclair's view.
Going hungry now and then, getting cold and working out hard are mild stresses that switch it on.
Sirtuins then tell cells to strengthen their defences and repair themselves without permanent damage.
Mammals have seven sirtuins, SIRT1 to SIRT7, involved in inflammation, energy metabolism and DNA repair.
Sirtuins need NAD+, a coenzyme whose levels fall with age.
His practical advice includes eating less often, skipping meals, less animal protein, high-intensity exercise, cold exposure and sauna.
Summaries note that parts of this rest on early animal research.

A synopsis of the advice lists skipping a meal, an eight-hour eating window, no food in the three hours before bed, occasional cold showers or ice baths, sauna and high-intensity intervals; sourced only to a secondary synopsis, so low.
Sinclair believes humans could live beyond 120, even 150, without the usual frailty; typical lifespan today is about 80 (medium).
Exercise is linked to longer telomeres and higher NAD levels (medium).
scene_details: a cold shower or cold exposure
seven sirtuins named SIRT1 to SIRT7
tension: A circuit built for famine and cold has little to do in a warm, fed life.
opening_idea: Open on the dormant alarm: a system built for hunger and cold that modern life rarely sounds.

lessons.idea: Use small deliberate demands for capacities that comfort lets fade
lessons.anchor: the survival circuit sitting dormant in modern comfort; Everyday: someone who always takes the lift and finds the stairs hard on the day it breaks

reflect_final: Where in your week does everything come easy, and what small, safe demand could you add there on purpose?

use_cases.situation: Friends plan another long dinner and drive
use_cases.move: Sinclair says the body's defences switch on with mild stress. Want to walk first, even twenty minutes, before we eat?

use_cases.situation: You notice you never skip a meal or climb a stair
use_cases.move: I have not asked my body for anything lately. This week I will try one small demand that my doctor would be fine with.

use_cases.situation: A parent asks what Sinclair's advice means for them
use_cases.move: He suggests skipping meals and cold exposure, but the evidence is partly from animals. Let's ask your doctor which part fits you.

pocket_idea: Sinclair says our survival circuit evolved for famine and cold. Give it one small, safe demand this week.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Sinclair thinks our bodies carry a famine-and-cold alarm that a warm, fed life seldom sounds.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Sinclair says every cell inherits a survival circuit, sirtuins, mTOR and AMPK, built for famine and cold. Modern life keeps it quiet. Mild stress such as a skipped meal, cold or hard exercise switches it on and sirtuins push cells to defend and repair. Parts of this rest on animal work, so treat it as his argument.
